Empirical Research Plan: Adjustment Costs and Efficiency Gains from the Canada-U.S. FTA

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with a continuous treatment intensity, complemented by an event-study (dynamic DID).

Rationale  
• Policy variation: The FTA generated clearly timed, legislated tariff schedules that differ in size across narrowly defined 4-digit Canadian SIC industries.  
• Clean setting: No simultaneous macro-stabilisation or privatisation programs.  
• Rich panel: 1980–1996 plant- and industry-level panels allow pre- and post-policy tracking and saturated fixed effects.  
• Continuous treatment DID captures heterogeneous treatment “doses” (size of the tariff cut) rather than a binary shock.  
A dynamic DID (leads/lags) provides visual and statistical pre-trend checks and estimates of short- vs. long-run effects.

Secondary checks  
• Triple-difference: compare Canadian industries to their U.S. counterparts (control for global sectoral trends).  
• Instrumental variables: use the mechanically determined U.S. tariff schedule as an instrument for Canadian tariff cuts to attenuate lobbying-related endogeneity (see Threat #1).

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Unit of analysis: i = industry (4-digit SIC) or plant p in industry i, year t.

Treatment variable  
TARiff_cut_i = (Tariff_i,1986 – Tariff_i,1996) / Tariff_i,1986  
Post_t = 1 from 1989 onward (anticipation year 1988 is dropped).

Core DID regressor  
TreatIntensity_it = TARiff_cut_i × Post_t  
Interpreted as the share-point reduction in Canadian MFN-weighted tariff on U.S. imports that has occurred by year t.

Control group  
Industries with zero or very small (<2 p.p.) negotiated cuts provide the within-Canada counterfactual. In robustness, we re-weight to match pre-FTA characteristics.

Exports side (efficiency gains)  
Define EXP_cut_i analogously for U.S. tariffs on Canadian products; include it jointly to separate import-competition (IC) and export-access (EA) channels.

Treatment timing  
Policy enacted 1 Jan 1989; linear phase-out (mostly 5-year, 10-year) ⇒ use yearly dose actually in force (CumCut_it). Leads t ≤ 1986, anticipatory lead t = 1987 serve for pre-trend tests.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: absent the FTA, high-cut and low-cut industries would have evolved similarly.  
– Plausibility: Negotiated schedules were reciprocity driven, not contemporary performance; still testable with 1980-86 leads.

A2. Exogeneity of treatment size: size of cut uncorrelated with unobserved shocks affecting outcomes after 1989.  
– Reasonable: tariffs historically reflect 1930s/1940s protection, not 1980s dynamics; use IV and controls.

A3. No interference across industries (SUTVA): changes in one industry do not spill over heavily to others.  
– Partially plausible; test via input–output linkages.

A4. Stable unit composition: plant entry/exit not differentially driven by unobserved factors correlated with tariff cuts beyond the tariff itself.  
– Plausible with rich controls; check using balanced vs. unbalanced panels.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Endogenous tariff concessions (lobbying by declining industries).  
Mitigation • Show weak pre-trend differentials.  
      • Instrument Canadian cuts with mandated U.S. cuts (reciprocity table) or gravity-predicted foreign tariff decline.

Threat 2: Differential demand shocks (e.g., U.S. recession 1990–91 hitting export-exposed sectors).  
Mitigation • Include industry-specific U.S. output growth as control.  
      • Triple-difference with matched U.S. industry outcomes.

Threat 3: Measurement error and mis-timing (effective vs. statutory tariffs).  
Mitigation • Use effective tariff (duty-collected / customs value) baseline.  
      • Robustness with statutory rates and lag/lead shifts.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
library(ivreg)      # 2SLS robustness
# ------------------ 1. Load data -------------------------
asm  <- read_csv("canada_asm_plants_1980_1996.csv")   # plant-year
tar  <- read_csv("tariff_schedule.csv")                # industry-level
us_tar<- read_csv("us_tariff_schedule.csv")
io   <- read_csv("input_output_links.csv")             # optional controls

# ------------------ 2. Merge & Construct ----------------
data <- asm %>%
  left_join(tar, by = c("sic4","year")) %>%
  left_join(us_tar, by = c("sic4","year"),
            suffix = c("_can","_us")) %>%
  group_by(sic4) %>%
  mutate(
    base_tar    = tariff_can[year==1986][1],
    cum_cut_ic  = pmax(0, base_tar - tariff_can)/base_tar,   # 0–1
    base_tar_us = tariff_us[year==1986][1],
    cum_cut_ea  = pmax(0, base_tar_us - tariff_us)/base_tar_us,
    post        = if_else(year>=1989,1,0)
  ) %>% ungroup()

# outcome example: log employment
data <- data %>% 
  mutate(log_emp = log(employment),
         treat_ic = cum_cut_ic * post,
         treat_ea = cum_cut_ea * post)

# ------------------ 3. Main DID specification -----------
# Plant × Year panel with industry & year FE
did_main <- feols(log_emp ~ treat_ic + treat_ea | sic4 + year,
                  data = data, cluster = ~sic4)
summary(did_main)

# Dynamic event study (5 leads/lags)
data <- data %>%
  mutate(rel_year = year - 1988) %>%           # 0 = immediate pre-policy
  filter(rel_year >= -5 & rel_year <= 7) %>%
  mutate(rel_year_fac = factor(rel_year))
es <- feols(log_emp ~ i(rel_year, cum_cut_ic, ref = -1) |
                         sic4 + year, data = data, cluster = ~sic4)
iplot(es)      # pre-trend visual

# ------------------ 4. IV robustness --------------------
iv_spec <- ivreg(log_emp ~ treat_ic + treat_ea | 
                 . - treat_ic + cum_cut_ea, data = data)
summary(iv_spec, diagnostics=TRUE)

# ------------------ 5. Placebo check --------------------
data_placebo <- data %>% filter(year<=1986) %>%
  mutate(fake_post = if_else(year>=1983,1,0),
         fake_treat = cum_cut_ic * fake_post)
placebo <- feols(log_emp ~ fake_treat | sic4 + year,
                 data = data_placebo, cluster=~sic4)
summary(placebo)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (Priors)
------------------------------------------------------------
• Employment: –3 % to –6 % in industries at the 75th percentile of tariff cuts within five years; effects attenuate to –2 % by 1996.  
• Labor productivity: +4 % to +8 % long-run due to exit of low-productivity plants and within-plant learning.  
• Real hourly wages: small decline (–1 % to –2 %) or neutral; composition shifts toward non-production & high-skill labour.  
• Import prices: fall roughly one-for-one with tariff reduction (pass-through 80 %–100 %).  
Theory: competitive pressure reallocates resources, boosting TFP but creating short-run adjustment costs in employment.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)
C1 Parallel trends verified by pre-policy leads .............................1  
C2 Exogenous treatment timing (policy shock) ................................1  
C3 No major interfering policies over study window ..........................1  
C4 Stable composition / no differential attrition ..........................0.5  
C5 No spillovers across units ..............................................0.5  
Total = 4/5 → credible but requires standard robustness work.
